about.label: About
about.heading: What is Thao Maha Brahma (Erawan Shrine)?
about.lead: A four-faced Brahma shrine in central Bangkok believed to answer prayers for career, love, health and study
about.paragraph1: Thao Maha Brahma (Erawan Shrine) stands at the corner of Ratchadamri and Phloen Chit roads, Pathum Wan, opposite CentralWorld and the Grand Hyatt Erawan. It was built in 1956 during the construction of the Erawan Hotel to dispel misfortunes that struck the project.
about.paragraph2: The image worshipped today is bronze, gilded in gold; the original 1956 image was plaster over a wooden core and was recast after the 2006 attack (see History below). The four faces represent creation, prosperity, protection and benevolence. Today it is one of Thailand's most famous sacred sites, free to visit daily 06:00–22:00.

rituals.label: Worship
rituals.heading: Worship customs & offerings
rituals.quote: With a focused mind and sincere faith, what you truly wish for shall come to pass
rituals.intro: Worship at Thao Maha Brahma follows long-standing traditions — the offerings, the clockwise walk and the dance troupes all carry meaning. Here is a basic guide for first-time visitors.

steps.title: Prepare the offering set (incense is placed, not lit)
steps.desc: Buy the standard set at the foundation stall inside the fence — 12 incense sticks, 4 garlands and 1 candle. Under the smoke-free worship policy, offerings are placed but never lit

steps.title: Walk clockwise around the shrine
steps.desc: Circle the shrine to the right (clockwise) and pause to pray at each face respectfully

steps.title: Pray at each face
steps.desc: Each face represents a different blessing; make a separate wish at each one

steps.title: Hire a dance troupe (when granted)
steps.desc: When a wish is fulfilled, devotees hire a dance troupe to perform as an act of gratitude

offerings.title: Flowers (jasmine, ylang, rose)
offerings.desc: Fragrant flowers are the basic sacred offering, often made into garlands

offerings.title: Incense, candles & joss powder
offerings.desc: 12 incense sticks, 4 garlands and 1 candle form the standard set. Offerings are placed but never lit — the shrine has been smoke-free since 2018

offerings.title: Fruit & ceremonial items
offerings.desc: Seasonal fruit and other items are placed on the offering table

offerings.title: Red cloth & donations
offerings.desc: Red cloth and donations are commonly offered for good fortune

rituals.dance: Dance troupes are hired to perform for the deity. When a wish is granted, devotees return to hire a troupe in gratitude. Some troupes have dozens of performers and several perform together in the evening, creating a beautiful and festive atmosphere.

history.label: History
history.heading: History & legends of Thao Maha Brahma (Erawan Shrine)
history.intro: From Hindu deity worship absorbed into Thai Brahmin rituals, this shrine grew from a small corner into a symbol of Bangkok

blocks.title: Origins (1956)
blocks.text: During construction of the Erawan Hotel several fatal accidents occurred. A Brahmin priest was consulted and a Brahma shrine was built in front of the hotel for good fortune; the misfortunes then ceased.

blocks.title: The four-faced belief
blocks.text: The four faces represent creation, long life, prosperity and protection. Worshippers walk clockwise and pray at each face in turn.

blocks.title: The 1994 incident
blocks.text: A mentally ill man smashed the image with a hammer; an angry crowd killed him. The original was preserved in a museum and a replica was made.

blocks.title: The current image
blocks.text: After a 2006 attack, a new bronze-and-gold image replaced the plaster one for durability, and it remains open for worship to this day.

legend.title: The legend of its sacredness
legend.text: It is said that those who pray with sincere faith and have their wishes granted often return to give thanks with dance troupes. This belief made the shrine one of Asia's most famous wish-making sites, especially among visitors from China, Hong Kong, Singapore and Taiwan.

didYouKnow.title: Did you know?
didYouKnow.text: Although Brahma is a Hindu deity, the shrine is maintained by Thai Brahmin ritual and is revered equally by Buddhists and Hindus.

folklore.title: Tales from the elders
folklore.tale: It is said Brahma is the creator god, so people offer flowers, scents and dance to show gratitude.
folklore.shrine: When life succeeds, they speak of the merit made at this shrine, and return to pray again and again.

faqs.q: Is entry free?
faqs.a: Entry is free, but offerings and dance troupes cost as chosen

faqs.q: What are the hours?
faqs.a: Open daily 06:00–22:00, good for both morning stops and evening prayer

faqs.q: What can I pray for?
faqs.a: Each face is believed to answer career, love, health and study; pray separately at each

faqs.q: How do I get there?
faqs.a: BTS Chit Lom Exit 1 is a ~5 min walk, or take a car/taxi to CentralWorld

faqs.q: What should I wear?
faqs.a: Not as strict as temples, but dress modestly and remove hats while praying

faqs.q: What time does Erawan Shrine close?
faqs.a: The shrine opens at 06:00 and closes at 22:00 every day, including public holidays. The last thanks-giving dance round stops taking bookings about 30 minutes before closing.

faqs.q: How much does a thanks-giving dance troupe cost?
faqs.a: Official foundation rates: 260 baht for 2 dancers, 360 baht for 4, 460 baht for 6 and 710 baht for 8, per performance. Book at the desk inside the shrine grounds only — outside troupes are not accepted.

faqs.q: Who manages Erawan Shrine?
faqs.a: The shrine is operated by the Than Tao Mahaprom Foundation (มูลนิธิทุนท่านท้าวมหาพรหม), which runs the official offering stalls and the dance troupe booking desk inside the fenced area.

faqs.q: Where can I find official information about the shrine?
faqs.a: The shrine is managed by the Than Tao Mahaprom Foundation; official tourism information about the site and district is published by the Tourism Authority of Thailand.

knowledge.title: Background: Phra Phrom vs Indra
knowledge.text: Phra Phrom (Brahma) is the creator god and the main image of this shrine; Indra rules the Trayastrimsa heaven and is a guardian deity who averts misfortune. The Ratchaprasong intersection is a sacred zone watched over by eight Hindu deities, and the Indra shrine in front of Amarin Plaza stands barely a hundred metres from the Erawan Shrine. That is why the on-site notice board also carries chants honouring and petitioning Indra — a sign of how inclusively these beliefs are blended.

chant.label: Chants
chant.heading: The Phra Phrom katha and opening invocation
chant.intro: The shrine's official texts are short katha — all of them fit on one screen and can be chanted standing up. Pick whichever suits you: the short form if you are in a hurry, the full katha if you want to do it properly.
chant.note: These chants are Thai phonetic renderings of Sanskrit and Pali, and spellings differ slightly between sources (for example พรหมเรสสะยัม and พรหมเวสสะยัม) without changing the sound. Sincere focus matters more than exact wording, so do not worry about mispronouncing.

blocks.title: 1. Opening invocation: the triple homage (Namo Tassa)
blocks.desc: The standard opening homage in Thai Buddhist and Brahmin rites, recited before any request.
blocks.thai: นะโม ตัสสะ ภะคะวะโต อะระหะโต สัมมา สัมพุทธัสสะ
blocks.roman: Namo Tassa Bhagavato Arahato Sammā Sambuddhassa
blocks.pronunciation: NA-mo TAS-sa pa-ka-wa-to a-ra-ha-to SAM-ma sam-put-TAS-sa
blocks.meaning: Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Fully Enlightened One.

blocks.title: 2. Main chant: the Phra Phrom katha (โอมปะระเมสะ นะมัสสะการัม)
blocks.desc: The most widely circulated official katha for the Erawan shrine. Reading all twelve lines once counts as one round.

lines.thai: โอมปะระเมสะ นะมัสสะการัม
โองการะ นิสสะวะรัง
พรหมเรสสะยัม ภูปัสสะวะวิษณุ
ไวยะทานะโมโทติ
ลูกะปัม ทะระมา ยิกยานัง
ยะไวยะลา คะมุลัม สะทา
นันตะระ วิมุสะตินัน
นะมัตเต นะมัตเตเร
จะ อะการัง ตโถวาจะ
เอตามา ตาระยัต ตะมัน ตะรามา
กัตถะ นารัมลา จะสะระวะ ปะติตัม
สัมโภ พะกลโล ทิวะทิยัม มะตัมยะ

blocks.pronunciationNote: Thai is a tonal language and the Roman line is the reliable reading aid. As an orientation, the opening line โอมปะระเมสะ นะมัสสะการัม sounds roughly like "ohm pa-ra-ME-sa na-MAT-sa-ka-ram".
blocks.meaning: This is an act of homage and refuge to Brahma: it opens with โอม (Om), the primordial sound, followed by นะมัสสะการัม, "I bow in reverence", and continues as a request for blessing, protection and grace. Because the whole text is a Thai phonetic rendering of Sanskrit, a reliable word-by-word translation has been lost in transmission; the accepted sense is simply an earnest homage to Brahma asking for blessing and protection.

blocks.title: 3. Short form: the Phra Phrom heart mantra (โอม พรหมมายะ นะมะห์)
blocks.desc: A single line — useful when you are short of time or cannot linger in the crowd.
blocks.thai: โอม พรหมมายะ นะมะห์

faces.heading: Four faces clockwise — what to ask at each
faces.intro: Start with the face you find yourself looking at as you enter, then move clockwise. The order should not be reversed, and you should never walk against it.

items.desc: Job hunting, promotion, exams, starting a business — direction and prospects

faces.tip: The four-face attributions are folk tradition and vary between communities. If you already follow a set order, pray in the way you know with a sincere mind — what matters is covering all four faces, not just one.

steps.label: Step by step
steps.heading: How to worship on site: six steps
steps.intro: From buying incense to returning a vow — follow these the first time you go.

items.title: Buy your offerings at the foundation stall inside the fence
items.desc: 12 incense sticks, 4 garlands and 1 candle, with prices clearly displayed. Do not buy from roaming vendors outside the fence.

items.title: Wash your hands, settle your mind, chant the homage three times
items.desc: Recite Namo Tassa three times and let your mind quieten before making a wish — devotees consider focus far more important than expensive offerings.

items.title: Start at the front face and go clockwise
items.desc: At each face place 3 incense sticks and 1 garland, put your palms together and state your name, date of birth and your wish.

items.title: Place the candle on the face you care most about
items.desc: There is only one candle, so put it on the face that matters most for this visit. Under current rules incense and candles are not lit.

items.title: Return to the front face and chant the main katha
items.desc: Walk back round to the first face, chant the katha 3 times (or 9), bow with palms together and you are done.

items.title: Come back to give thanks when the wish is granted
items.desc: Devotees believe a promise made must be kept. See "Offerings & vows" below for the options.

offerings.label: Offerings & vows
offerings.heading: Offering set and how to return a vow

set.note: Placed on the face you care most about. Some stalls sell sets with 4 candles — one per face is also acceptable

offerings.elephantNote: Wooden elephants are the most common thanks-offering, and the larger the size the greater the thanks. Buy them at the foundation stall inside the fence; sizes over 40 inches are not accepted.
offerings.danceTitle: Thanks-giving dance (ละครชาตรี)
offerings.danceNote: Hiring a dance troupe once your wish is granted is the shrine's most famous form of thanks. Rates are set and posted by the foundation, and bookings must be made inside the shrine — outside private troupes are not accepted.
offerings.danceFlow: The person giving thanks kneels in front of the troupe, the lead dancer announces their name and what was granted, and the dancers perform to traditional Pi Phat music. Each round lasts under 15 minutes.

taboos.label: Etiquette
taboos.heading: What not to do at the shrine

items.title: Incense and candles are never lit
items.desc: Under the city and foundation smoke-free initiative, offerings may be placed but not lit.

items.title: Do not release birds you brought yourself
items.desc: This is an explicit current rule, with a 500 baht fine for violations.

items.title: Walk clockwise, never against the flow
items.desc: Going anticlockwise is considered disrespectful and blocks other worshippers.

items.title: Dress modestly and remove your hat to pray
items.desc: Less strict than a temple, but avoid very revealing clothing.

items.title: Do not pose with your back to the image
items.desc: Folk belief holds that turning your back on the image is disrespectful. Also avoid photographing people mid-prayer.

items.title: Folk custom: avoid beef before worshipping
items.desc: This circulates among devotees and is not an official rule. If it matters to you, skip beef the day before.

items.title: Wishes should be fair and harm no one
items.desc: Devotees widely hold that a request that profits by harming others will not be answered.

items.title: Keep the promise you made
items.desc: Whatever form of thanks you promised while wishing must be carried out — this is the single most important principle here.

faqs.q: How many times should I chant the Erawan Shrine prayer?
faqs.a: Recite the Namo Tassa homage 3 times, the main Phra Phrom katha 3 or 9 times, and the short heart mantra 4 times. If you are short of time, four rounds of the short mantra is enough — focus matters more than the count.

faqs.q: Can I chant if I do not speak Thai?
faqs.a: Yes. The text is a Thai phonetic rendering of Sanskrit and Pali, so simply follow the Roman transliteration. Devotees generally hold that sincerity and focus matter more than perfect pronunciation.

faqs.q: What should I pray for at each of the four faces?
faqs.a: Starting from the face you meet as you enter and going clockwise: career and study, then love and relationships, then wealth, then health and safety. These attributions are folk tradition and vary between communities, so simply make sure you cover all four faces.

faqs.q: Do I have to come back and give thanks?
faqs.a: In the prevailing belief, yes — the form of thanks you promised while making the wish must be carried out. Common options are a wooden elephant, hiring a dance troupe, or a donation, depending on how big the wish was and what you can afford.

faqs.q: How long does a prayer visit take?
faqs.a: Around 15 to 30 minutes for the worship itself. In the evening, when thanks-giving troupes perform back to back, expect to stay longer and to find it more crowded.

faqs.q: Are the offerings sold on site a rip-off?
faqs.a: The foundation stalls inside the fence display fixed prices and are the safe place to buy. Vendors outside the fence often sell the same set at several times the price — do not buy from them.

meta.title: How to Get to Erawan Shrine: BTS Chit Lom, Skywalk & Airport Transfers
meta.description: Step-by-step directions to Erawan Shrine in Bangkok: BTS Chit Lom Exit 1, the Ratchaprasong skywalk, MRT, taxis and transfers from Suvarnabhumi and Don Mueang airports.

hero.title: How to get to Erawan Shrine
hero.subtitle: The shrine sits on the traffic island at Ratchadamri and Phloen Chit, opposite CentralWorld. The BTS Sukhumvit Line is the easiest way in — here is every option, from the airport to the kerb.

sections.heading: By BTS Skytrain
sections.lead: The Sukhumvit Line runs directly overhead. Chit Lom station is the closest; Siam is a short skywalk walk away.

items.title: BTS Chit Lom — Exit 1 (recommended)
items.desc: Leave by Exit 1 and walk south along Ratchadamri Road towards CentralWorld. The shrine is on the traffic island at the Phloen Chit corner, about 5 minutes on the flat. Follow the crowd — this is the route almost every visitor takes.

items.title: BTS Chit Lom — Exit 4 / skywalk
items.desc: Exit 4 connects to the elevated Ratchaprasong walkway (see the skywalk route below). No traffic lights to cross, useful with luggage or in the rain.

items.title: BTS Siam
items.desc: One stop north. Cross to CentralWorld on the elevated walkway and continue south — about 10 minutes in total, and often less crowded than Chit Lom concourse.

items.title: BTS Phloen Chit
items.desc: One stop north of Chit Lom. Walk south on the skywalk or along Ratchadamri — about 12 minutes. Only worth it if your hotel is on that side.

sections.heading: The Ratchaprasong skywalk route (no road crossing)
sections.lead: Ratchaprasong is one of Bangkok's busiest intersections. The elevated walkway keeps you off the roads entirely.
steps: From Chit Lom station, follow the signs for CentralWorld / skywalk up to the elevated concourse (Exit 4).
Walk south over the Ratchaprasong intersection on the skywalk — you pass above the roads, with views down onto the shrine.
Descend at the CentralWorld corner near Gaysorn Village; the shrine is on the traffic island directly below.
Total time from platform to shrine: about 8–10 minutes, fully step-free with escalators and lifts.

sections.heading: Other lines & buses
sections.lead: No rail line stops closer than Chit Lom, but there are workable combinations.

items.title: MRT Blue Line — Lumphini station
items.desc: About 1.5 km south. Take a taxi or motorcycle taxi for the last stretch (10–15 minutes), or bus 77/165 along Ratchadamri.

items.title: MRT Blue Line — Si Lom station
items.desc: Walk or taxi north to Sala Daeng, then BTS Silom Line one stop to Siam and the skywalk south — usually slower than a direct taxi.

items.title: Chao Phraya Express Boat
items.desc: Get off at Sathorn pier, then BTS Silom Line to Siam and the skywalk — about 50 minutes door to door, and the slowest option. Nice only if you are already on the river.

items.title: BMTA buses
items.desc: Lines along Ratchadamri and Phloen Chit stop near the intersection (e.g. 13, 16, 77, 165). Fares are cheap but traffic on this corridor is heavy at peak hours.

sections.heading: From Suvarnabhumi (BKK) and Don Mueang (DMK)
sections.lead: Both airports connect to the BTS network; budget roughly an hour door to door from BKK and 40–60 minutes from DMK.

items.title: From Suvarnabhumi (BKK)
items.desc: Airport Rail Link to Phaya Thai (about 30 minutes), transfer to the BTS Sukhumvit Line and ride to Chit Lom (about 10 minutes), then Exit 1 and walk 5 minutes. Total fare is roughly 100 baht and the whole trip takes about an hour.

items.title: From Don Mueang (DMK)
items.desc: Take the A1 shuttle bus to BTS Mo Chit (about 30 minutes), then the Sukhumvit Line south to Chit Lom. Alternatively a taxi via the tollway takes 40–50 minutes and around 300–400 baht depending on traffic.

items.title: Taxi or ride-hailing from either airport
items.desc: About 300–450 baht from BKK and 250–400 baht from DMK, plus tolls. Use the official taxi queues or an app; set the destination as 'Erawan Shrine' or 'CentralWorld' and ask to be dropped at the Ratchadamri corner.

items.title: Late-night arrivals
items.desc: BTS trains stop around midnight; after that a taxi or ride-hailing is the only practical option. The shrine itself is closed to visitors after 22:00.

sections.heading: By taxi, ride-hailing & car
sections.lead: The shrine is on a traffic island, so drop-off points matter more than the entrance.

items.title: Where taxis can stop
items.desc: Drivers drop passengers at the Ratchadamri/Phloen Chit corner by CentralWorld. Ask for 'ศาลท้าวมหาพรหม' or 'Erawan Shrine'; most drivers know the corner even if they say the shrine is 'inside' the island.

items.title: Parking
items.desc: No parking at the shrine itself. Use CentralWorld, Gaysorn Village or Amarin Plaza car parks and walk over via the skywalk or the ground-level crossing.

items.title: Traffic warnings
items.desc: Ratchaprasong gridlocks at rush hour (08:00–09:30 and 17:30–20:00). If your time is tight, the BTS is faster and cheaper than sitting in a car.

items.title: Walking from nearby hotels
items.desc: The Grand Hyatt Erawan is next door, and the Siam/Chit Lom hotel area is 5–15 minutes on foot. The skywalk makes the walk safe and shaded.

faqs.q: Which BTS station is closest to Erawan Shrine?
faqs.a: BTS Chit Lom on the Sukhumvit Line, Exit 1 — about a 5-minute walk. Siam station also works via the CentralWorld skywalk, about 10 minutes.

faqs.q: How do I walk from BTS Chit Lom to the shrine?
faqs.a: Leave by Exit 1, walk south along Ratchadamri Road towards CentralWorld, and the shrine is on the traffic island at the Phloen Chit corner. There is no need to cross the big intersection at street level if you use Exit 4 and the skywalk.

faqs.q: Can I reach Erawan Shrine by MRT subway?
faqs.a: Not directly. The nearest MRT station is Lumphini (Blue Line), about 1.5 km away — take a taxi or bus for the last stretch. The BTS Sukhumvit Line is the practical choice.

faqs.q: How do I get from Suvarnabhumi Airport to Erawan Shrine?
faqs.a: Airport Rail Link to Phaya Thai, transfer to the BTS Sukhumvit Line to Chit Lom, then walk from Exit 1. The trip takes about an hour; a taxi is about 300–450 baht plus tolls.

faqs.q: How do I get from Don Mueang Airport to Erawan Shrine?
faqs.a: Take the A1 shuttle bus to BTS Mo Chit and ride the Sukhumvit Line to Chit Lom, or take a taxi via the tollway for 40–50 minutes.

faqs.q: Is there parking at Erawan Shrine?
faqs.a: No. The shrine occupies a traffic island. Park at CentralWorld, Gaysorn Village or Amarin Plaza and walk over via the skywalk.

meta.title: Erawan Shrine Offerings & Dance Prices: What to Buy and What It Costs
meta.description: What to offer at Erawan Shrine and what it costs: the 12-incense offering set, garlands, candles, wooden elephants and the foundation's posted thanks-giving dance rates, checked October 2026.

hero.title: Offerings, wooden elephants & thanks-giving dance rates
hero.subtitle: Entry to Erawan Shrine is free; what you spend on offerings and thanks-giving is up to you. Here is exactly what the foundation's stalls sell and what the posted rates are.

sections.heading: The standard offering set
sections.lead: One set covers a full clockwise round. Offerings are placed at each face — under the smoke-free policy nothing is lit.

rows: 3 sticks at each of the four faces — placed, never lit
1 at each face; jasmine and ylang are the usual flowers
Placed on the face you care most about; some stalls sell sets of 4
Dabbed on the offering table or your palms
Tied to the shrine railing as part of the wish

sections.note: Prices start from about 20 baht for a basic set; fuller sets with all of the above cost more. Everything is sold at fixed prices at the foundation's stall inside the fence.

sections.heading: Where to buy — and what to avoid
sections.lead: Buying in the right place is the single best way to avoid overpaying at this shrine.

items.title: The foundation stall inside the fence
items.desc: Located just inside the entrance. Fixed prices are displayed, the sets are complete, and this is also where thanks-giving dances are booked. This is the only place you need.

items.title: Roaming vendors outside the fence
items.desc: They sell similar sets at several times the official price, sometimes with pressure to buy. Decline politely and walk to the stall inside.

items.title: Bringing your own flowers
items.desc: You may bring flowers bought elsewhere, but complete sets are cheapest and simplest from the foundation stall.

sections.heading: Thanks-giving dance (Lakhon Chatri) rates
sections.lead: Hiring a dance troupe is the shrine's most famous way of returning a vow. Rates are set and posted by the foundation and must be booked inside the shrine.

rows: Ask at the booking desk inside the shrine

sections.note: Rates compiled from the foundation's posted notices, checked October 2026; prices may change. Each round lasts under 15 minutes and runs during opening hours (06:00–22:00). Private troupes from outside are not accepted.

sections.heading: Wooden elephants for returning a vow
sections.lead: Wooden elephants are the most common thanks-offering; size is read as the weight of the gratitude.

rows: Buy only at the official stall inside the shrine

sections.note: Prices compiled from the foundation's posted notices, checked October 2026; prices may change.

sections.heading: Common scams around the shrine
sections.lead: The shrine area attracts touts. A few simple rules keep the visit trouble-free.

items.title: 'Lucky strings' and blessing demands
items.desc: People may approach offering to tie a string on your wrist for luck, then ask for a large donation. Decline politely and walk away; blessings are not sold here.

items.title: Marked-up offerings outside the fence
items.desc: The same garlands and incense cost several times more from vendors outside. Buy inside the fence only.

items.title: Paid 'official' photos
items.desc: Anyone charging for photographs of the shrine is not connected to the foundation. Taking photos is free.

items.title: Bird release requests
items.desc: Releasing birds you brought yourself is explicitly prohibited, with a 500 baht fine. Do not buy birds for release.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to make an offering at Erawan Shrine?
faqs.a: Entry is free and a basic offering set of flowers, incense and candles starts from about 20 baht at the foundation's stall inside the fence. What you spend beyond that is voluntary.

faqs.q: How much is a thanks-giving dance at Erawan Shrine?
faqs.a: The foundation's posted rates are 260 baht for 2 dancers, 360 for 4, 460 for 6 and 710 for 8, per round of under 15 minutes. Book at the desk inside the shrine; outside troupes are not accepted. Rates checked October 2026.

faqs.q: Do I have to light the incense and candles?
faqs.a: No. Under the smoke-free worship policy observed since 2018, offerings are placed but never lit. This applies to incense, candles and joss powder.

faqs.q: Can I bring my own offerings?
faqs.a: Yes, though complete sets are cheapest from the foundation stall inside the fence. Anything you bring must still comply with the smoke-free rule and the size limits on wooden elephants.

faqs.q: How big can the wooden elephant be?
faqs.a: Up to 40 inches. The foundation's stalls sell sizes from 13 inches (500 baht) to 40 inches (2,000 baht); anything larger is not allowed because it blocks space for worshippers.

faqs.q: Are the prices on this page guaranteed?
faqs.a: They were compiled from the foundation's posted notices and checked in October 2026. Prices can change — confirm at the stall or booking desk on the day of your visit.
